summary:
Lunar Compass is an interactive lunar landing-site planning platform that helps explorers evaluate possible locations near the Moon’s south pole. Users can select coordinates on a 3D lunar globe and analyze Sun and Earth visibility across a mission window using NASA JPL Horizons apparent-airless observer data. The platform combines this with NASA LOLA terrain screening, source-backed nearby water-ice reference sites, historical lunar mission context, and multi-site comparison tools.

It addresses the challenge of turning complex lunar data into an understandable decision-support experience for students, mission planners, and researchers. By showing illumination, communication visibility, terrain constraints, and resource proximity in one place, Lunar Compass makes the trade-offs of lunar landing selection easier to explore. It is important because reliable access to sunlight, Earth line-of-sight, terrain information, and polar resources will shape safer, more informed future lunar exploration.
details:
Lunar Compass is an interactive decision-support platform for exploring potential lunar landing sites, especially in the challenging south-polar region. A user selects a point on a 3D Moon interface or enters east-positive lunar coordinates. The system then evaluates the site across a chosen UTC mission window and presents the results in a clear mission-planning view.

The core Sun and Earth Visibility Engine requests apparent-airless observer ephemerides from NASA JPL Horizons for the Sun and Earth as seen from the lunar surface. It samples each hour at the exact midpoint and calculates four practical metrics: sunlight percentage, Earth visibility percentage, longest darkness period, and longest Earth-visibility gap. This helps users understand illumination and line-of-sight trade-offs without claiming to predict terrain-safe operations or mission success.

Lunar Compass also includes local screening of NASA LOLA terrain data for elevation, slope, and roughness proxies; source-backed nearby water-ice reference sites; historical lunar mission information; site comparison; and an optional exploration assistant. The platform keeps scientific limitations visible: it does not fabricate missing data, terrain screening does not replace hazard analysis, and geometric visibility does not guarantee communication, power, or landing safety.

The project benefits students, researchers, and future mission planners by bringing multiple difficult-to-interpret lunar datasets into one understandable visual workflow. Its intended impact is to make lunar science data more approachable while encouraging evidence-based discussion about where and when exploration may be more viable.

We developed Lunar Compass using Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, HTTPX, NumPy, Rasterio, JavaScript, Three.js, Vite, HTML, and CSS. We used NASA JPL Horizons, NASA LOLA data products, NASA technical-reference sources, and publicly documented historical mission sources. The backend is designed for deployment with Render, while the frontend is deployable as a static web application.

The creative element is the combination of an explorable 3D lunar globe with a scientific planning engine. Instead of showing raw tables alone, Lunar Compass lets users move from a visual location on the Moon to transparent calculations, source context, limitations, and comparative trade-offs in one experience.
